rows: The front eyes resolve fine detail, about 12.5 cycles per degree in Portia fimbriata, and that sharpness belongs to a strip only a few degrees wide. The rest of the picture is blurred.
The side eyes take in close to 360 degrees of the world together. The rear and side views are wide and dim, and they pick up movement first.
The principal eyes of Saitis barbipes carry an ultraviolet class near 359 nm and a green class near 526 nm, so the picture is shown in those two pigments rather than in full colour.
The principal retinae swing side to side and rotate, so the sharp strip sweeps across the scene and returns. A stationary target does not start a saccade on its own.
The side eyes respond to moving things and go quiet to still ones, so still things fade in this picture. How far they fade is the app's choice.
The strength of the glow, its colour, the fade of still things, the hold of a moment and the dimming with light are the app's own choices, and no record gives their values.

rows: A bottlenose dolphin resolves about 2.4 to 4.8 cycles per degree in the records, and a humpback whale about 3.3 to 3.95. A harbour seal calculates to 8.7 to 11.5. We blur the picture to about 4.
Whales and seals carry only one kind of cone, so they see along one channel with no separate colours. Their peak sensitivity lies between about 488 and 520 nanometres, a blue-green band.
A bottlenose dolphin has a panoramic field of 120 to 130 degrees, with the two eyes overlapping only 20 to 30 degrees.
Most whales and seals have a reflective layer behind the retina, which gives dim light a second pass. Dolphins and seals on the records show it, so the picture glows a little in low light.
The sharpness, colour mapping, pupil shape and dim-light gain are the app's own choices, built on the records above. No record gives the pupil or the gain for these animals.

The value 125 is the middle of the 120 to 130 degree panoramic field given for bottlenose dolphins and dolphins.
The reflective tapetum on cetaceans and the tapetum fibrosum in bottlenose dolphins support a sheen, graded g because it is a wider group statement.

The matrix is a single channel with weights chosen by the app, built on one cone class and the pigment peaks in the records; the matrix itself is graded i, so this claim is limited to the one-cone statement.

rows: A honeybee resolves a grating of about 0.26 cycles per degree, and a bumblebee about a quarter of a cycle. A person resolves about 60, so the bee view is very soft and small things melt away.
Each compound eye reaches about 156 degrees back from straight ahead, so the two eyes together cover close to 300 degrees around. Only a small blind region lies below and behind the bee.

A bee has three kinds of colour receptor, with peaks near 344 nm in the ultraviolet, 436 nm in the blue and 556 nm in the green. Far red falls outside what bees see. This view shifts colours so that ultraviolet shows as blue, blue as green and green as red, which is one common way to draw a bee's view.
A honeybee can still tell flicker apart at about 200 flashes a second in bright light, and a bumblebee at about 130. At 300 lux the honeybee figure falls to 144.
The colour shift maps the three bee receptors onto the three colours a phone can show. The flicker speed-up of three times is a rough stand-in for a bee's fast flicker fusion.

rows: Scorpions can apparently see 360 degrees around the body. The pair of median eyes in the middle of the carapace is reported to cover the full circle, with about 40 degrees of overlap above the animal where both eyes look at the same place.

Recordings from the eyes of two scorpions, Tityus macrochirus and Centruroides edwardsii, peak in blue light at 470 nm and in green light at 525 nm. Other work puts the main peak near 500 nm, and the lateral eyes have a smaller peak in ultraviolet between 350 and 400 nm. Earlier studies suggest the receptors form one population most sensitive to green, so the colours here are a loose guide.

The scorpion's eyes work at starlight levels, and scorpions are active at night. In Androctonus australis the median eyes are about 3 log units more sensitive at subjective night than by day, and the lateral eyes are about 1 log unit more sensitive than the median eyes at night.

The median eyes are described as the main eyes, with relatively high acuity and good spatial discrimination. The lateral eyes may only detect changes in light. No one has measured the detail a scorpion sees in cycles per degree.
The leg sensors of sand-dwelling scorpions respond to waves in the sand made by moving insects as far as 50 centimetres away. A sand scorpion can find a cricket by this feeling alone.
A male Centruroides margaritatus courts a female with a judder through the ground. Each pulse lasts about 0.018 seconds, with gaps of about 0.028 seconds. The phone buzzes in that beat.

The sharpness and the brightness of the picture, the strength of the pulse at the screen edge, and the way the two colour peaks become screen colours are the app's own choices. The records give no figure for these.
A scorpion tastes with its comb-like pectines and feels the direction of wind with fine hairs. The camera records neither.

rows: Whales, dolphins and seals tested so far carry only the long-wavelength kind of cone and have lost the blue-sensitive kind. A bottlenose dolphin's cone pigment peaks between 522 and 524 nanometres. We show the picture the way a single kind of cone would, which leaves almost no colour. A few behaviour tests hint that dolphins can tell two wavelengths apart, and manatees have two cone kinds, so this is the usual case for the group and has exceptions.

Rorquals, right whales, bowhead whales, sperm whales and beaked whales have lost the genes for both kinds of cone pigment. They see with rods alone, and their rod pigments peak between about 483 and 499 nanometres, in the blue-green part of the spectrum.

Estimates of how fine a detail these animals resolve run from about 2.6 to 3.3 cycles per degree in several toothed whales and 3.3 to 4.8 in baleen whales. A harbour seal comes in near 11.5 under water and a manatee near 1.6. We blur the picture to 3.95, a humpback whale's estimate, which is far less sharp than your own view.
A wide view with little overlap
A dolphin's eyes sit on the sides of its head. Together they cover 120 to 130 degrees, and the two eyes overlap by only 20 to 30 degrees. We leave the field as your camera gives it.

A bottlenose dolphin was half a log unit more sensitive than a person in dim light and a little less sensitive in bright light. Bottlenose dolphins, many whales and seals have a reflecting layer behind the retina that gives light a second pass. Manatees have none. We lift the shadows strongly and add a modest sheen.

A bottlenose dolphin makes clicks between 40 and 150 kilohertz and builds a picture from the echoes. A harbour seal can follow the trail of a fish through the water with its whiskers up to 35 seconds after the fish has passed. A phone cannot give either sense, so they are left out of this view.

One sharpness of 3.95 stands for the whole group, one dolphin pigment peak stands for every species, the brightness gain is worked out from one dolphin test, and the strength of the reflecting sheen is a guess.

rows: Most monkeys and apes have three kinds of colour sensor. Owl monkeys and bushbabies have only one kind of cone, so they see no colour, and some New World monkeys have two.
A rhesus monkey reaches about 26 cycles per degree and a marmoset is estimated near 30, against a person's 60. Mouse lemurs are far less sharp, near 4 to 5.
Owl monkeys are nocturnal and see without colour. Marmosets, rhesus monkeys, capuchins and chimpanzees are active by day.
Owl monkeys have only a rudimentary fovea, while squirrel monkeys and macaques have a clear fovea with dense cones at its centre.

The picture is blurred to about 12 cycles per degree, a little more than a bushbaby would show and well below the monkeys' best, and the sharp middle is drawn at a scale of 2.2. These are the app's choices and the records give no exact figure.

claims.how: The app picked 12 cycles per degree as a point between the cited macaque figure of 26.3 (R7) and the 21.4 cycles per degree worked from 1.4 arc minutes (R12), with the marmoset's estimate of 30 (R2) as a ceiling; this is worked out and invented, and graded g.

rows: A macaque has three kinds of cone, most sensitive near 430, 531 and 561 nanometres. That is close to your own three, so colours look much as they do to you.

A rhesus monkey reaches about 26 cycles per degree by seven weeks of age, close to a person's 30. A marmoset's cone mosaic could carry about 30 near the fovea. A grey mouse lemur manages only about 4 to 5.

Owl monkeys have a single cone type, lack colour vision and are active at night. Male marmosets have two cone types. Howler monkeys are fully trichromatic. This view shows the three-cone pattern of macaques.
Macaques, squirrel monkeys and marmosets have a clear fovea, a small pit where vision is sharpest. Owl monkeys have only a rudimentary one. We draw no separate sharp centre.
Neurons in macaque visual cortex respond to the small difference between the two eyes' images, which supports stereoscopic depth. A phone has one camera, so this view leaves that cue out.
The single sharpness of 26 is the app's pick from a wide spread of measured values. The colour matrix is the app's mapping from three pigment peaks. The colour drawing is the app's own.

claims.how: The value equals the 26.3 cycles per degree that rhesus monkeys reached, which was the highest level the test assessed.
The matrix name stands for a matrix built from the peaks 430, 531 and 561 nm that R31 gives for a cynomolgus monkey, with R32 giving 530 nm and R23 giving 561 nm.
The peaks 430, 531 and 561 nm come from R31, and each lies within 2 nm of a cited peak (430 R31, 530 R32, 561 R23).

rows: A scorpion has a median pair of eyes in the middle of the carapace and lateral eyes along each side. Lateral eye pairs number five in many buthid scorpions, and median and lateral eyes together give a view that reaches all round the body.

Scorpion eyes peak in blue light near 470 nm and in green light near 525 nm, and they respond to ultraviolet with a smaller peak. The view keeps these colours and mutes red, which the records say scorpions are weakly sensitive to.
Scorpions are nocturnal, and their eyes respond to starlight levels of light, so the picture lifts dim scenes and dims bright ones.
A scorpion finds much of its food and its way with the hairs and slits on its legs, the pectines and the palps. The camera records none of these, so the picture shows only what the eyes would.
No record gives how much detail a scorpion sees. The view is coarse, with the middle a little sharper, and still things fade partly so that movement and light stand out.
Vibrations through sand and air, and the touch of the legs, carry much of what a scorpion knows, and the screen shows none of them.

claims.how: Both records give a full 360 degree field, so the whole-animal field is set to 360.
